name: Yousician
tagline: Listens to you play guitar, piano, bass, ukulele or sing, and scores you note by note against a scrolling song chart.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The technical heart of Yousician, real-time pitch detection from a microphone scored against a scrolling note chart, is genuinely a weekend build now. Web Audio plus a decent monophonic pitch tracker gets you a working practice game for single notes, scales and melodies, and you can feed it your own MIDI files. What you cannot build is the thing people actually subscribe for: a catalog of licensed songs people recognise, arranged in difficulty tiers, plus a curriculum that decides what you practice next. Polyphonic chord detection, strum detection and the mobile app experience are also where the one-sitting version falls apart. So you get a very good practice metronome with ears, not a replacement for the product.
coreLoopDIY: Loads a MIDI melody, scrolls it as a note highway, listens to your instrument through the mic, and scores each note for pitch and timing with a running accuracy readout.
requirements: A microphone or audio interface, and a quiet-ish room
MIDI files or MusicXML for anything you want to practice, you supply your own
Node 20 and a Chromium browser for the Web Audio bits
whatYouLose: The licensed song catalog, which is the actual product for most subscribers
Reliable chord and strum detection, your DIY build will handle one note at a time and nothing else
A curriculum that sequences exercises by skill and nags you at the right difficulty
Polished iOS and Android apps, plus progress sync across devices
Latency tuning and instrument-specific calibration that took them years to get right
moatNotes: Pitch detection is a solved math problem in the public domain. Song licensing for a few thousand recognisable tracks across five instruments is not, and neither is a decade of data on where learners stall.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because nobody practices scales generated by their own weekend project. People pay for the dopamine of playing a song they know, correctly, with a score at the end, and that requires rights to the song. The pedagogy matters too: being told exactly which three exercises to do today is worth more than a tool that will score anything you point it at. A self-hosted note highway is excellent for drilling a specific piece you already have sheet music for, which is a real but much narrower use.
notes: The ear is free, the songbook is not. Build this if you already know what you want to practice.
prompt:
Build a local-only browser app called "Practice Highway": a real-time instrument practice trainer.

Stack, no substitutions: Vite + TypeScript + vanilla DOM, canvas for rendering, Web Audio API for input. Use the "pitchy" npm package for pitch detection and "@tonejs/midi" for MIDI parsing. No backend, no accounts, no telemetry, no cloud. Everything runs on localhost.

In scope:
1. A file picker that accepts a .mid file and extracts the first monophonic melody track as a list of { midiNote, startSeconds, durationSeconds }.
2. A canvas "note highway": notes scroll right to left toward a fixed judgement line, vertical position mapped to pitch, width mapped to duration. 60fps, requestAnimationFrame, time-based not frame-based.
3. Mic capture via getUserMedia with echoCancellation, noiseSuppression and autoGainControl all set to false. Run pitchy's McLeod pitch method on an AnalyserNode buffer each frame. Discard results below a clarity threshold of 0.9.
4. Convert detected frequency to a MIDI note number plus cents offset. Draw a live pitch indicator dot on the highway so the player sees themselves tracking the line.
5. Scoring: for each chart note, sample detected pitch across its window. Score "clean" if within 50 cents for 70% of the window, "close" if within 100 cents, else "miss". Show a running accuracy percentage and a per-note result strip at the end.
6. Tempo control: 50% to 100% playback speed, and a loop-section control with draggable start and end markers, because that is how practice actually works.
7. A built-in exercise generator: major and minor scales, chromatic runs, and interval drills in any key, generated as charts without needing a MIDI file.
8. Persist per-chart best accuracy and a practice streak in localStorage. Add a JSON export button.
9. A calibration step that measures input latency: play a click, have the user tap or pluck on it, compute the offset, store it, and subtract it from all scoring windows.

Out of scope, do not attempt: polyphonic chord detection, strum or rhythm-guitar scoring, licensed song content, any audio downloads, user accounts, mobile wrappers.

If any secret is ever needed, read it from .env and ship a .env.example. Write a README explaining that you must supply your own MIDI files, and why chord detection is deliberately absent.
